name: Esther Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Esther, thank you for doing this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a water truck at the Kerrow bauxite mine, the red-dirt one out past the grain silos. I spray the haul roads all shift so the dust doesn't blind the truck drivers or get into everyone's lungs, and I fill up at the standpipe every forty minutes or so. It sounds simple, but you have to get the amount right: too little and there's dust, too much and a truck slides off the road. I'm still learning that, and the shift supervisor has had words with me twice. I like being out in the open, and I pray in the cab when the road's quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Daniel and I have a small cattle place, about four hundred acres, and two dry years and the beef price put us badly behind with the bank. I'd been keeping house and doing the parish office, but we needed real wages, so I applied here at fifty-six. We've less than a month's bills put by, and most of my pay goes to the farm loan. I use the AI on my phone every single day, by the way: for studying my truck ticket, the parish newsletter, the farm books, everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and get on with the day. At church I'd say the Lord gave us brains for a reason and it's still our job to use them. I'd probably write something light about it in the parish newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little sorry, because I like what it does for me. The AI helped me pass my truck ticket at fifty-six. I'd hate for people to decide it was all hype because it didn't take over the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, keep studying for the next ticket so I can move onto haul trucks, which pays more. I'd keep using AI for the farm books to get on top of the loan. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit relieved for the others at work who were scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI helped you pass your truck ticket. How did that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd photograph the pages of the handbook and ask it to quiz me on the bus to the mine. When I got something wrong it explained it until I understood. I passed first try, and two of the young men didn't, which I won't pretend I didn't enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving onto haul trucks mean for the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and twenty more a week, all of it onto the bank loan. That's maybe two years off the debt. Daniel would sleep better, and so would I.

S0.say: She'd say 'that's that' and get on with the day, telling church friends it's still our job to use our God-given brains, and perhaps write a light piece in the parish newsletter.
S0.think: She'd be a little sorry, because AI helped her pass her truck ticket at fifty-six and she doesn't want it dismissed as hype.
S0.do: Keeps driving and studies for a haul truck ticket worth about a hundred and twenty more a week. Uses AI for the farm books to get on top of the bank loan.
S0.feel: Calm, and relieved for frightened colleagues.
S0.quote: The AI helped me pass my truck ticket at fifty-six. I'd hate for people to decide it was all hype because it didn't take over the world.
S0.fieldNote: Esther is a traditional, church-going farm wife who is also the most enthusiastic AI user on her crew. She credits it with passing her ticket at fifty-six and enjoyed beating the young men. Her money goal is concrete: every extra dollar goes onto the farm loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has every right to run its business the best way it can, and it's up to us to make ourselves useful. I'd tell the women at work to start learning now. I'd not complain, complaining never paid a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A water truck is the easiest thing in the world to automate, it just follows the roads and sprays. If I'm honest, my job is a sprinkler on wheels, and I'd be surprised if they need me in five years. So I'd want to be on the other side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask straight away about the control room where they run the self-driving trucks, and do whatever course gets me there, using AI to study. I'd also start selling eggs and preserves online from the farm, which I've been meaning to do. And I'd keep every spare dollar going to the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of the loan, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the other side of it'. Do you really think they'd put a fifty-eight-year-old in the control room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why not? I'm the one already using these programs every day. The young men can drive faster, but I can read a screen and I don't panic. If they don't pick me, I'll ask what I'd need to do to be picked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, on the grader. He's sixty and he won't touch a phone, he says it's the devil's toy. I've offered to help him and he says no thank you. I'd keep offering, and I'd pray for him.

S1.say: She'd say the company has every right to run its business as it sees fit and that workers must make themselves useful, urging the women at work to start learning now.
S1.think: She thinks her water truck is the easiest job to automate, a sprinkler on wheels, and wants to be on the control-room side of the change.
S1.do: Asks straight away about the self-driving truck control room and takes any course to get there, studying with AI. Starts selling eggs and preserves online and keeps putting every spare dollar on the farm loan.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly because of the farm loan rather than the robots.
S1.quote: If I'm honest, my job is a sprinkler on wheels, and I'd be surprised if they need me in five years.
S1.fieldNote: Esther combines free-market views ('the company has every right') with a cheerful plan to move first. She is blunt about her own job, calling it a sprinkler on wheels. Her unease comes from the farm debt, not fear of technology, and she keeps trying to help a colleague who refuses phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other, as they always have. I'd say don't sit and wait for the government. I'd say it in the newsletter, gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, two years scares me more than I'd admit at church. I can learn fast, but not faster than the bank can take the farm. With no savings and the loan, we'd be in trouble quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for any job running or looking after the new machines, at the mine or anywhere nearby, and study every night. I'd push the online egg and preserves business hard. And I'd sit down with our son and daughter-in-law about whether they could help with the loan, or take on part of the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot, but I'd still feel like I could do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AGI can do almost any work, what makes you think there'd be jobs looking after the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At first there will be, someone has to set them up and keep an eye on them while people still don't trust them. It might only last a couple of years. But a couple of years of wages is the difference between keeping the farm and losing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be thinking about Daniel in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's sixty-one and he's never done anything but cattle. If they've got robots that can muster and fence, what does he do? I think he'd be lost, and I'd have to be the strong one. I've done it before, when his father died.

S2.say: She'd say families and churches must carry each other as always, and that people shouldn't sit and wait for the government.
S2.think: She thinks two years scares her more than she'd admit: she can learn fast, but not faster than the bank could take the farm.
S2.do: Applies for any job running or looking after the new machines and studies every night. Pushes the online egg business and asks her son and daughter-in-law to help with the loan or take on part of the farm.
S2.feel: Anxious and praying a lot, but still feeling able to act.
S2.quote: I can learn fast, but not faster than the bank can take the farm.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture is where Esther's confidence meets the bank, and she names that limit clearly. She'd rely on family rather than government, consistent with her views. She expects machine-minding jobs to last only briefly, but sees even a couple of years of wages as worth fighting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so there's no excuse for not getting ready. I'd say learn something, save something, look after your neighbours. I'd put a list of free courses in the parish newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me sixty-three. Five years is long enough for me to pay down the farm, learn the control room, and be the grandmother who knows how the robots work. I'm quite hopeful about it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the haul truck ticket and apply for the control room training, studying with AI on the bus. I'd start saving properly once the extra pay comes, even fifty a week. And I'd build up the online farm shop so it's a real income by the time the mine changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the control room actually involve, as you picture it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting in a room in town watching screens that show where every truck is, and stepping in when one gets confused. I've seen photos of it on the mine's notice board. It's mostly reading and patience, and I'm good at both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd sacrifice to do all of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the parish work, which I'd hate. I'd hand the newsletter to someone younger, or let the AI write a first draft and just check it. Sundays I'd keep, that's not negotiable.

S3.say: She'd say five years is fair warning with no excuse not to prepare, telling people to learn, save and look after neighbours, and list free courses in the newsletter.
S3.think: She's hopeful that five years is enough to pay down the farm, learn the control room and become the grandmother who knows how the robots work.
S3.do: Gets the haul truck ticket in the first year and applies for control room training, studying with AI on the bus. Saves about fifty a week once the extra pay arrives and builds the online farm shop into a real income.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to pay down the farm, learn the control room, and be the grandmother who knows how the robots work.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Esther's energy returns, and her plan stacks a better ticket, retraining and a side business. She would give up some parish work but not Sundays. Her picture of the control room is concrete and drawn from what she's seen on the mine notice board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, plenty of time to get ready. I'd say young people should be learning these machines now, alongside a trade. At church I'd say there's no need to be afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be sixty-eight, and I'd probably stop before it fully arrives. With ten years I'd get the farm clear, retire on my own terms and still have time to boss the robots around a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the haul truck ticket, then the control room, at a normal pace. We'd clear the farm loan over the decade and start saving for retirement. I'd keep the online farm shop going for something to do later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your grandchildren in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn the machines and the land both, so they can run the farm with robots instead of losing it to someone who has them. My granddaughter's eleven, she's already better with the AI than I am. I'd encourage that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about it that does trouble you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether people will still need each other, I suppose. If machines do all the work, what happens to the church working bees, the neighbours helping at branding time? I think we'd have to work hard to keep that, on purpose.

S4.say: She'd call ten years a blessing, urging young people to learn the machines alongside a trade and telling her church there's no need to be afraid.
S4.think: She thinks at sixty-eight she'd likely stop before AGI fully arrives, having cleared the farm, retired on her own terms and still had time to boss the robots around.
S4.do: Takes the haul truck ticket and then the control room training at a normal pace. Clears the farm loan over the decade, starts saving for retirement and keeps the online farm shop going.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd get the farm clear, retire on my own terms and still have time to boss the robots around a bit.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Esther see a full arc: clear the farm, learn the new work and retire on her terms. Her one real worry is about community, whether people will still need each other once machines do the work. She wants her grandchildren to master both the land and the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the bank wouldn't wait while I learned something new. What would help is the banks giving farm families a breathing space on loans when the jobs change, and the mine training older workers like me for the control room, not just the young ones. And keep the apprenticeships for the youngsters.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about faith. People think a church lady can't love a computer, but I pray on the bus and then ask the AI to quiz me on my ticket. I don't see why it has to be one or the other.

headlineQuote: People think a church lady can't love a computer, but I pray on the bus and then ask the AI to quiz me on my ticket.
portrait: Esther Young is 58 and drives a water truck at the Kerrow bauxite mine, a job she took at fifty-six when dry years and low beef prices put her family's cattle farm behind with the bank. She has less than a month saved, and most of her pay goes on the farm loan. She is traditional and devout, and also uses AI every day; it helped her pass her truck ticket. She's calm or uneasy in the milder pictures, planning to move into the control room and sell farm produce online. Two years of warning makes her anxious because the bank wouldn't wait, but with five or ten years she's hopeful about clearing the farm and retiring on her own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the bank wouldn't wait while she learned something new and the farm could be lost.
whatWouldHelp: Banks giving farm families breathing space on loans when jobs change, and the mine training older workers for the control room as well as young ones.
